sources.title: Prince of Wales Northern Heritage Centre: Giant Beaver on the Weledeh River

sources.title: Prince of Wales Northern Heritage Centre: Yamoria Place Names Map

sources.title: Prince of Wales Northern Heritage Centre: Dene Laws

sources.title: Cannon, Herbert, and Sangris, Stellar Wayfinding among Indigenous Peoples of the North American Arctic
sources.note: Pages 183 to 186 document Fred Sangris's learned Yellowknives practices with stars, landmarks, cairns, family teaching, and weather limits.

sources.title: Cannon, Herbert, and Sangris, Yellowknives Dene and Gwich'in Stellar Wayfinding

sources.note: Pages 79 to 81 synthesize late eighteenth and early nineteenth century posts, Yellowknives range, Akaitcho, conflict, trade, and later change.

sources.title: Parks Canada: Thanadelthur national historic person
sources.note: Official account of a Dene woman interpreter and negotiator, 1715 to 1717 peace, regional copper reports, and trade context.

sources.title: Library and Archives Canada: Samuel Hearne journal
sources.note: Archival description of Hearne's 1770 to 1772 journey with Matonabbee and Dene companions to the Coppermine River.

sources.title: Library and Archives Canada: Sir Alexander Mackenzie journal
sources.note: Archival description and provenance of Mackenzie's 1789 northern journey and its surviving journal transcript.

sources.title: Helm and Gillespie: Akaitcho, Arctic 36
sources.note: Peer reviewed profile separating Akaitcho's documented 1820s leadership, Yellowknives geography, provisioning, violence, rescue, and later dispersal.

sources.title: Yellowknives Dene First Nation: Language, Culture and History
sources.note: First Nation page describing living Wiilideh and Tetsot'ine languages as carriers of knowledge, skills, identity, health, and culture.

sources.title: Jaker: Tetsot'ine Prefix Vowel Length
sources.note: Peer reviewed community supported description of Tetsot'ine Yatie, speakers, dialect status, research methods, and modern linguistic notation.

sources.title: National Endowment for the Humanities: Yellowknife Verb Grammar Award
sources.note: Public grant record for modern collaborative documentation of the endangered Yellowknife language variety and planned verb grammar.

sources.title: Cooper and colleagues: Native Copper Provenance in the Arctic and Subarctic
sources.note: Peer reviewed archaeological study distinguishing regions, sources, exchange, and precontact copper use, including Wiilideh and Tetsot'ine associations.

sources.title: Akaitcho Dene First Nations Framework Agreement
sources.note: Parties' agreement identifying current constituent First Nations, asserted land relationships, distinct culture, and continuing negotiation.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.name: T'atsaot'ine
proposedOverrides.summary: T'atsaot'ine, or Copper People, connects to Yellowknives Dene history around Great Slave Lake; the atlas polygons are badly misplaced.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact missing record is t-atsaot-ine, indexed once as T'atsaot'ine with Yellowknives alias from 1530 to 1815.
The label is treated as a people and cultural history, not the centralized state kind imported by the basemap pipeline.
Living Yellowknives Dene communities and historic T'atsaot'ine relationships overlap but are not reduced to one timeless membership list.
All fifty border snapshots were audited; seven exact features occur in seven files and form five unique decoded geometries.
Every exact target polygon excludes Yellowknife, Dettah, and Ndilo; the 1715, 1783, and 1800 versions retain only a distant eastern Arctic component.
The 1530 to 1815 interval is map coverage, not a foundation or extinction chronology.
Later oral histories and museum objects are labeled as remembered knowledge or comparison rather than silently back-projected facts.
No secure contemporaneous written-language sample exists for the exact people and window; later orthographies and outsider spellings are not substituted.
The 1815 endpoint is a Canada repaint and continuity, with fell null and no invented successor association.
